intro.heading: The Imperial Ancestral Temple
intro.body: The Mieu is the Citadel temple where Hue's Nguyen emperors are honored. Come for red lacquered altar space, incense, tiled roofs, and the Nine Dynastic Urns beside the courtyard.

sections.heading: Altars Inside The Citadel
sections.body: This is one of the clearest places to remember that the Citadel was tied to worship as well as government. Move more quietly here than you might in the open palace courtyards.

sections.heading: Look Beside The Courtyard
sections.body: The Nine Dynastic Urns stand nearby, each made to honor a Nguyen emperor. See the temple and urns together so the courtyard turns royal memory into something physical.

sections.heading: Ask Before Close Photos
sections.body: Temples can have different expectations from open landmarks. Ask before close photos, especially near altars or worship areas.

sections.heading: Keep The Pace Quiet
sections.body: Let the courtyard slow down a little: tiled roofs, red lacquer, incense, and people moving with more care than in the busier palace halls.

relatedSubtitles.label: Cửu Đỉnh
relatedSubtitles.subtitle: The bronze urns beside the temple courtyard, with royal detail in one slow circle.
relatedSubtitles.proof: The bronze urns beside the temple courtyard, with royal detail in one slow circle.

intro.heading: The Pagoda Above The River
intro.body: Thien Mu Pagoda is Hue's famous Buddhist pagoda above the Perfume River. Look for the seven-tier tower, temple gates, incense, worship areas, and the river sitting just below the grounds.

sections.heading: Tower, Courtyard, River
sections.body: The tower is the postcard image, but the visit is also a temple courtyard. Give yourself time for incense, gates, shaded corners, and the river view below.

sections.heading: Good With A River Ride
sections.body: A Perfume River boat ride makes more sense when it lands somewhere memorable. Thien Mu gives the ride a clear destination instead of only open water.

sections.heading: More Than The Tower
sections.body: Do take the tower photo, then keep walking. The gates, worship areas, and river edge connect the pagoda to Hue beyond the scenic view.

sections.heading: Ask Before Close Photos
sections.body: A pagoda is an active religious place, so wide photos are easier. Around worship areas, altars, or monks, ask before taking close photos.

intro.heading: A Quieter Imperial Tomb
intro.body: Thieu Tri Tomb honors Emperor Thieu Tri, one of Hue's Nguyen emperors. Expect a quieter countryside tomb with walls, gates, stone paths, open ground, and low mountain views.

sections.heading: Countryside Around The Tomb
sections.body: This tomb does not crowd you with palace rooms. The open ground, walls, gates, and mountain edge carry much of the visit.

sections.heading: After The Famous Tombs
sections.body: If you have already seen Minh Mang or Tu Duc, this one gives a quieter comparison. There is more room to notice countryside space, old walls, and the approach.

sections.heading: Open Space Matters
sections.body: Picture low tomb structures, stone paths, old walls, and countryside air. It is calmer than a crowded monument courtyard.

sections.heading: Come For Space
sections.body: The reason to remember Thieu Tri is the open setting around royal history. Choose it when you want a tomb visit with less spectacle and more air.

intro.heading: Pomelo Trees Near The River
intro.body: Thuy Bieu is a river village near Hue known for garden houses and pomelo trees. It is a gentle way to see lanes, walls, bicycles, small markets, and the Perfume River outside the imperial core.

sections.heading: Pomelo Lanes And Garden Houses
sections.body: This is a lane-and-garden visit: pomelo trees, leafy paths, low walls, bikes, and quiet houses near the Perfume River.

sections.heading: After Tombs Or Pagodas
sections.body: After imperial gates, tombs, or pagodas, the village gives the day something lived-in. The shift is simple: houses, gardens, river air, and smaller roads.

sections.heading: What To Notice
sections.body: Look for pomelo fruit, garden walls, shaded lanes, bicycles, and small local markets. Those details separate Thuy Bieu from the Citadel.

sections.heading: Keep The Route Simple
sections.body: Know where to start, how long you want to walk or ride, and where the pickup happens before you wander deeper into the lanes.

intro.heading: Incense Craft Before Color
intro.body: Thuy Xuan Incense Village is a Hue craft village where bright incense displays lead back to real handwork: bamboo sticks, scented paste, dyed colors, and drying racks.

sections.heading: Watch How It Is Made
sections.body: Watch how the incense is rolled before taking close photos or shopping. If someone invites a try, you get a small craft lesson rather than just a backdrop.

sections.heading: Morning For Softer Light
sections.body: Morning often gives softer light on the incense displays. It also keeps the ride easier before the tomb route west of Hue gets hot.

sections.heading: Pair It With The Tomb Route
sections.body: Thuy Xuan sits on the west side of Hue, near routes people use for royal tombs such as Tu Duc or Dong Khanh. Add it when the day already points that way.

intro.heading: Imperial-Style Hue At The Table
intro.body: Tinh Gia Vien is a garden-house restaurant for Hue's imperial-style cuisine, the careful court-influenced cooking tied to the Nguyen emperors. The meal moves through carved wood, courtyard greenery, composed dishes, and a slower rhythm than an everyday local lunch.

sections.heading: The Garden Sets The Pace
sections.body: A quick bowl of noodles shows one side of Hue. This table shows another: courtyard shade, woodwork, careful plating, and the older dining manners that grew around the royal city.

sections.heading: Ask What To Order
sections.body: The menu is about composed Hue dishes, more than quick hunger. Ask for the house direction, then let the table move more slowly than a casual food crawl.

sections.heading: Outside Seating Matters
sections.body: A table near greenery or courtyard detail changes the meal. Outside, the restaurant's garden-house side is easier to read: shade, old-house texture, and a little room between courses.

sections.heading: Court Taste At Table Scale
sections.body: The flowers and carved vegetables are part of the appeal. The deeper context is Hue's royal food tradition, brought down to table scale through presentation, pace, and small composed dishes.

intro.heading: The River Boarding Point
intro.body: Toa Kham Boat Station is where central Hue turns from streets into Perfume River boats. Expect steps down to the water, boat noses at the edge, bridge views nearby, and the small but real work of confirming fare and boarding point.

sections.heading: Before The River Turns Scenic
sections.body: A boat ride sounds simple from home. On the riverbank, the details become physical: which steps, which boat, which operator, what price, and where the return will happen.

sections.heading: Confirm The Fare First
sections.body: Boat prices and routes can blur in conversation at the river edge. Confirm the fare before stepping down, especially if the ride is private or loosely arranged.

sections.heading: Street To Water
sections.body: Traffic drops behind you, the Perfume River opens in front, bridge lines cross the view, and boats rock close enough to make the route feel real.

sections.heading: Match The Pier Name
sections.body: Ben thuyen means boat pier. Match the Vietnamese name, location, and route before boarding so a river plan stays clear at the water's edge.

intro.heading: The Bridge That Places Hue
intro.body: Truong Tien Bridge is the pale steel bridge over the Perfume River that helps central Hue click into place. Its six arches, evening lights, and everyday crossings make the river feel like the city's middle.

sections.heading: Six Arches Over The River
sections.body: The shape is easy to remember: a long steel bridge with repeated arches stretched across the Perfume River. Once you know it, taxi rides, walks, and river photos have a center point.

sections.heading: Evening Changes It
sections.body: At night the bridge lights make the river feel more like a city stage. It is an easy landmark to notice after dinner, a boat ride, or a walk along the riverbank.

sections.heading: A Useful Photo Question
sections.body: The bridge is a public landmark, and the clearest angles often come from a riverbank, boat, or nearby crossing. Ask before using a shop, cafe, or private edge for the photo.

sections.heading: More Marker Than Monument
sections.body: Let the bridge become the marker that helps Hue's river, market side, and hotel side make sense together. It can work as a quick look, an evening walk, or a return-point image.

intro.heading: Indoor Reset Near The River
intro.body: Truong Tien Plaza is a central Hue shopping center near the river and Truong Tien Bridge. Air-conditioning, stores, food counters, bathrooms, and a clear meeting point make it useful when heat or rain starts shaping the day.

sections.heading: A Mall With A Travel Job
sections.body: Think less luxury shopping, more predictable indoor recovery. Cool air, a bathroom, a snack, a bag, or a card-friendly counter can keep the next outdoor plan from falling apart.

sections.heading: Small Asks Matter Here
sections.body: Card payment, bag, and bathroom phrases are the right scale for a shopping center. Those small asks can keep the group moving when heat, rain, or tired feet start to take over.

sections.heading: Between River Plans
sections.body: Its location near the river and bridge makes it easy to use between outdoor plans. Meet here, cool down, handle one errand, then move back toward the market, Citadel, or river walk.

sections.heading: Mall Air, Market Food
sections.body: Dong Ba Market gives central Hue texture and food browsing. Truong Tien Plaza gives the cleaner indoor reset when the group needs convenience, bathrooms, and easy meeting instructions.

intro.heading: The Tomb That Feels Like A Retreat
intro.body: Tu Duc Tomb is the mausoleum complex of Emperor Tu Duc, a Nguyen ruler of Vietnam. The complex reads like a royal retreat as much as a tomb: lake edge, pavilions, pine shade, old walls, courtyards, and stone paths.

sections.heading: Lake, Pavilions, Shade
sections.body: Water, pavilions, trees, paths, and courtyards slow the visit down before the tomb architecture takes over. The setting carries the story alongside the gates and halls.

sections.heading: Give One Tomb Enough Time
sections.body: Tu Duc can carry a full morning or afternoon on its own. Give the lake, pavilions, paths, and courtyards enough time to build the mood.

sections.heading: The Lake Edge Matters
sections.body: Picture moss, stone steps, calm water, and pine shade around the pavilions. The landscape guides the walk as much as the gates do.

sections.heading: The Emperor's Retreat Mood
sections.body: The lasting image is the combination: emperor's story, lake, trees, walls, pavilions, and a layout made for lingering. It is royal history with air, shade, and water around it.

intro.heading: Thich Nhat Hanh's Root Temple
intro.body: Tu Hieu Pagoda is an active Buddhist monastery on Hue's west side and the root temple of Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen teacher and peace activist known around the world. Expect pine shade, moss, temple gates, incense, courtyards, and slower movement.

sections.heading: Pine Shade And Monastery Life
sections.body: The pagoda works through calm details: a gate, tiled roofs, shaded paths, incense, and monks moving through a working monastery.

sections.heading: Between Tombs And Hills
sections.body: Tu Hieu sits naturally on a west-Hue day with Tu Duc Tomb, Vong Canh Hill, or Thuy Xuan Incense Village. It gives that route a calm religious center.

sections.heading: Ask Before Close Photos
sections.body: This is an active monastery, so wide photos are easier. Around worship areas, altars, or monks, ask before taking close photos.

sections.heading: The Name Carries Care
sections.body: Tu Hieu is often connected with filial piety, the Vietnamese value of care and respect for parents. That gives the calm courtyards more meaning than shade alone.

intro.heading: Pines Above The Perfume River
intro.body: Vong Canh Hill is a modest viewpoint near Hue's royal-tomb route. The hill gives you pine shade, Perfume River bends, countryside light, and a short climb that makes west Hue feel wider than tomb gates and walls.

sections.heading: Pines Above The River
sections.body: The hill is low, but the view opens around pines, the Perfume River below, and tomb-route landscape beyond the city center.

sections.heading: Soft Light Helps
sections.body: Late afternoon gives the river and pines more shape. Arrive while there is daylight for the climb, the view, and the ride back.

sections.heading: Plan The Ride Back
sections.body: This is outside the central river walk. Confirm the distance, the walking reality, and the pickup point before settling into the view.

intro.heading: A River Neighborhood With A Poem
intro.body: Vy Da is a lived-in Hue neighborhood near the river, with small lanes, houses, cafes, homestays, and local food edges. Vietnamese readers may also know the name from Han Mac Tu, a 20th-century poet whose famous poem remembers Vy Da village.

sections.heading: Lanes Instead Of A Monument
sections.body: Expect small lanes, river-adjacent houses, cafes, and everyday errands around the river. Let it fit into a nearby hotel stay, meal, or evening walk.

sections.heading: The Name Helps With Bearings
sections.body: Vy Da is an area with lanes rather than a front gate. The name helps connect a cafe, homestay, food stop, or evening walk into one mental map.

sections.heading: Poetry Without A Museum
sections.body: Han Mac Tu's poem gives the name a cultural echo, but the neighborhood is still ordinary life: houses close to the street, river air, food signs, and people moving through the day.

sections.heading: Good For A Softer Evening
sections.body: After Citadel gates or tomb routes, Vy Da can make Hue feel softer and more residential. Let it be a neighborhood walk, a dinner area, or an easier route back.

intro.heading: Hue After The Monuments
intro.body: Hue Walking Street is the easy evening version of the city: river air along Nguyen Dinh Chieu, plus busier food-and-drink streets around Pham Ngu Lao, Chu Van An, and Vo Thi Sau. Expect signs, vendors, cafes, crossings, and a looser night rhythm.

sections.heading: River Walk Or Night Streets
sections.body: Hue has more than one walking-street mood. The riverside stretch stays gentler; Pham Ngu Lao, Chu Van An, and Vo Thi Sau bring more food, drinks, signs, and night movement.

sections.heading: After Dinner Is Plenty
sections.body: After dinner, a full attraction may be too much. Walk once, choose a snack or cafe edge, then decide if the night needs more.

sections.heading: One Slow Pass First
sections.body: A slow first pass keeps the evening easy. Look for food stalls, cafe seats, music, crossings, and the river side before choosing where to stop.

sections.heading: Check The Local Timing

intro.heading: A Meal In An Old Hue House
intro.body: Y Thao Garden is a restaurant in an old Hue house inside the Citadel area, with garden seating, lanterns, woven mats, ceramics, wood furniture, and traditional Hue dishes. Ask what the kitchen recommends before building the table.

sections.heading: House Before Restaurant
sections.body: The old-house setting comes first: garden paths, shaded corners, ceramics, wood furniture, and a table that feels more like a family house than a standard dining room.

sections.heading: Ask What The Kitchen Likes
sections.body: This is a house-dish meal with time around it. Ask what the kitchen likes, then build the table around shared Hue dishes.

sections.heading: Outside Seating Changes It
sections.body: A garden or courtyard table changes the meal. Shade, house texture, and old-Hue calm sit around the plates instead of feeling like decoration.

sections.heading: Compare Garden Meals
